rv.q: The wonder of the performance lies in the way Crouch appears to point back at what he’s done, drawing our attention to the architecture of the action.

This extraordinary show is absolutely, extremely and very deliberately contrived: a slippery, shape-shifting duet that keeps changing the rules of engagement — with the material, with the premise, with the audience.
And as they stumble over unfamiliar lines, he performs a magic trick: transforming their real discomfort into the crackling tension between two characters bound together by grief and guilt.
Yet tonight it does feel more contrived than revelatory.
Yet the incontrovertible fact is that these 75 minutes of drama are a little too pleased with themselves – more pleased than we spectators will ever manage to be.
The parallels between an actor lost on stage and a man lost in mourning are just one of the play’s many masterstrokes.
Despite the premise oozing potential, what may have seemed novel 20 years ago, now looks a little half-baked, even embarrassing in places.
It’s ingenious and agile throughout, to be sure, but was I moved in any particular way, or myself emotionally transformed?
All in all, the production is a truly curiosity-inspiring watch that could be genuinely brilliant with more consideration

cn.t: Critics are divided on An Oak Tree's 20th anniversary revival—enthusiasts call it a theatrical wonder, skeptics find it contrived. All agree its unrehearsed guest-star format remains its boldest, most polarizing feature.
